title: English Vocabulary 4 · Units 49–50
description: Advanced advertising and journalistic vocabulary, with promotional claims, news gathering, editorial framing, newsroom collocations, register and media usage.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal vocabulary study from the user-supplied published reference material. Target selection follows its teaching pages, exercises and answer key. Portuguese translations, teaching notes and examples were independently written; original exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Complete teaching sections A–F of Unit 49 and A–B plus the Language help box of Unit 50, exercises 49.1–49.4 and 50.1–50.5, illustration-supported media-format items, and corresponding answer-key entries.
audit.pronunciation: Conservative broad British IPA is supplied where confident for individual words or short targets; uncertain or longer targets intentionally have blank IPA rather than speculative transcriptions. Connected speech and accent variants are not comprehensively transcribed.
audit.languagePolicy: Learner-facing labels, titles, examples, notes, objectives and metadata are in English. Brazilian Portuguese is confined to pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Reviewed the source study pages, layout/illustrations, exercises and answer key; checked the lexical coverage, advertising claims versus evidence, journalistic register, meaning contrasts, original examples, Portuguese translations, IDs, schema and static audio-target rules. Static JSON validation performed.
audit.limitations: No bundled MP3 audio. Actual VocabLab UI import, browser TTS pronunciation and speech recognition were not tested. The source reflects the 2017 textbook and some advertising or media conventions may change with time and location.

units.title: Unit 49 — Advertising
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 49. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Media and marketing · advertising claims, persuasive register and formats
learningObjectives: Recognise advertising claims about exceptional quality and value, including exaggeration and fixed expressions.
Use luxury, comfort, scientific credibility and attractiveness vocabulary with appropriate collocations.
Distinguish promotion channels and formats, from billboards and trailers to sponsorship and online pop-ups.
Identify advertising-only wording in the exercises and distinguish claims from independently verified facts.

sectionsChecked: A–E: quality, value, luxury, scientific backing and attractiveness, including definitions and collocations
F: advertising media, promotional formats and the meaning of plug
Exercises 49.1–49.4 and Unit 49 answer key, including image-based advertising formats

items.pt: dar uma olhada em; conferir (um produto)
items.example: Check out our new range of noise-cancelling headphones before the launch.
items.note: Informal imperative often used in promotions to attract attention to a product.

items.example: The manufacturer highlighted the innovative features of its compact camera.
items.note: Innovative implies new and original, but in advertising it can be a promotional claim.

items.example: An innovative design helped the device stand apart from its competitors.
items.note: Describes a new or original approach; often paired with design, solution or feature.

items.example: The company describes its customer service as unsurpassed in the industry.
items.note: Strong advertising superlative claim: allegedly as good as or better than anything else.

items.pt: superar os concorrentes com grande vantagem
items.example: The advert claims that the new engine will leave competitors standing.
items.note: Idiomatic comparative claim meaning be far better; its superiority is not independently established by the phrase.

items.example: The campaign promised a battery that would put competitors in the shade.
items.note: Put or leave something in the shade means make it appear much less impressive.

items.example: The clearance event was promoted with rock-bottom prices on selected items.
items.note: Informal, emphatic price language; the modifier is hyphenated before a noun.

items.example: The retailer plans to slash prices to clear its remaining inventory.
items.note: Slash means cut very sharply; it is common in headlines and advertisements.

items.example: The shop window promised bargains galore during the bank-holiday sale.
items.note: Galore means in large numbers; it follows the noun, unlike most English adjectives.

items.pt: um desconto; uma redução de preço
items.example: Customers receive a discount when they renew their subscription early.
items.note: Offer or get a discount; distinguish a genuine price reduction from a claimed bargain.

items.pt: bom custo-benefício; vantagem em relação ao preço
items.example: Independent reviewers praised the device for offering excellent value for money.
items.note: Refers to the relationship between cost and benefits, not merely a low purchase price.

items.example: The hotel invites guests to pamper themselves with a spa treatment.
items.note: Promotional phrase encouraging indulgent comfort or special treatment.

items.pt: permitir-se um prazer; entregar-se a um mimo
items.example: You can indulge yourself with a rich dessert after the celebration.
items.note: Indulge in something or indulge yourself with something; a pleasure may be excessive.

items.example: The restaurant advertised a sumptuous meal with several carefully prepared courses.
items.note: Sumptuous is especially natural with meals, food, interiors and furnishings.

items.example: Guests dined in opulent surroundings decorated with marble and velvet.
items.note: Opulent refers to obvious wealth and luxury, particularly a setting or lifestyle.

items.pt: no auge do luxo; cercado de conforto
items.example: The brochure promises a week in the lap of luxury at a secluded resort.
items.note: Fixed idiom meaning in extremely comfortable and expensive conditions.

items.example: The chair is ergonomically designed to support a comfortable working posture.
items.note: Refers to design informed by how people physically use a product, not a guarantee that it prevents pain.

items.pt: com eficácia comprovada por estudos médicos (alegação)
items.example: The advertisement says the treatment is medically proven, but it provides no study details.
items.note: A scientific-sounding marketing claim; appropriate evidence must be evaluated separately.

items.example: The campaign claims the supplement can boost energy levels throughout the day.
items.note: Boost means increase or improve; a promotional claim does not establish medical effectiveness.

items.example: The manufacturer demonstrated its state-of-the-art production equipment.
items.note: Fixed hyphenated adjective for the most advanced technology currently available.

items.example: The brand referred to scientific backing without identifying any published research.
items.note: Backing is evidence or support; the expression itself does not prove that a claim is reliable.

items.example: The bright yellow design helps the product stand out in the crowd.
items.note: Idiomatic expression meaning attract attention by being noticeably different.

items.pt: chamar a atenção; fazer as pessoas olharem
items.example: The designer hoped the unusual jacket would turn heads at the exhibition.
items.note: Informal idiom meaning attract favourable or surprised attention through appearance.

items.example: The advert showed a tantalisingly appealing selection of handmade chocolates.
items.note: Tantalisingly suggests a strong temptation or desire; distinctly persuasive register.

items.pt: de modo tentador; de forma irresistivelmente sugestiva
items.example: The preview revealed only a tantalisingly small part of the finished design.
items.note: Adverb from tantalise; a tempting prospect may remain just out of reach.

items.example: The shampoo advertisement featured a model with glossy hair.
items.note: Glossy describes a smooth, shiny appearance; the promotional image is not proof of product results.

items.pt: pele radiante; pele com aspecto saudável e luminoso
items.example: The campaign promised radiant skin after weeks of regular use.
items.note: Radiant suggests healthy-looking brightness; a frequent beauty-advertising collocation.

items.example: The brand aired a TV commercial during the championship final.
items.note: A commercial is a paid advertising spot; not a news broadcast.

items.example: The seller placed a classified ad for her second-hand bicycle.
items.note: Short advertisement grouped by category in print or online listings.

items.example: The motorway billboard promoted a new electric vehicle.
items.note: Large outdoor advertising board; distinct from a small poster or flyer.

items.example: The theatre distributed flyers to publicise its autumn programme.
items.note: Single promotional sheet handed out or displayed to advertise an event.

items.pt: trailer; prévia promocional de filme ou programa
items.example: The cinema released a short trailer for the upcoming documentary.
items.note: Preview advertising a film or broadcast; different from a full programme.

items.example: The company expanded its sports sponsorship through a regional cycling team.
items.note: A brand financially or materially supports a sport or team in exchange for promotional exposure.

items.pt: anúncio em formato de faixa; banner publicitário
items.example: A banner advertisement appeared across the top of the website.
items.note: Banner can describe a long promotional strip in physical or digital media.

items.pt: publicidade escrita no céu por fumaça de avião
items.example: Spectators noticed the sky-writing above the beach during the festival.
items.note: Advertising text formed in the sky, typically by aircraft smoke.

items.pt: placa publicitária vestida na frente e atrás do corpo
items.example: An employee carried a sandwich board advertising the café opening.
items.note: Two boards attached front and back to a walking advertiser; not a food-related board.

items.example: The shop printed its logo on every reusable carrier bag.
items.note: British English for a shopping bag used to carry purchases; can provide brand visibility.

items.example: The redesigned logo appears on all company packaging.
items.note: A distinctive brand symbol, not necessarily the full company name.

items.pt: anúncio que surge em uma janela ou sobreposição
items.example: The browser blocked a pop-up ad that covered the article.
items.note: An on-screen advertisement appearing unexpectedly in a new window or overlay.

items.pt: promover um produto em aparição pública
items.example: The actor used the interview to plug her latest documentary.
items.note: Informal verb plug means promote publicly, sometimes during an ostensibly unrelated appearance.

items.example: The shop advertised colossal discounts on last season’s coats.
items.note: Colossal is an emphatic exaggeration commonly used to promote value.

items.pt: digno de um rei; extremamente luxuoso
items.example: The hotel brochure described its suite as fit for a king.
items.note: Figurative claim of exceptional luxury or quality; not literal royal suitability.

items.example: The company claimed its latest screen would outshine competing displays.
items.note: Outshine means be more impressive or successful; a strong promotional comparison.

items.pt: dar-se um mimo; permitir-se um agrado
items.example: Go on and spoil yourself with a quiet weekend away.
items.note: In advertising, spoil yourself invites a treat; not the sense of making a child badly behaved.

items.example: The package was marketed as offering outstanding value for families.
items.note: Value claim emphasises benefits relative to price; outstanding is strongly favourable.

items.example: The advertisement described the new evening wear as tantalisingly elegant.
items.note: A marked advertising-style combination appealing to attractiveness and desire.

units.title: Unit 50 — The news: gathering and delivering
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 50. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Media and journalism · reporting process, newsworthiness and framing
learningObjectives: Distinguish print, broadcast, online and citizen journalism, and how sources promote stories.
Use newsroom collocations for press conferences, soundbites, deadlines, copy and story publication.
Explain editorial language including scoops, airtime, column inches, gloss, spin and muck-raking.
Recognise journalistic register, defamation terminology and the grammar of media as a plural or modifier.

sectionsChecked: A: journalism types, newsgathering, numbered definitions and publicity collocations
B: newsroom production, publication, opinion, allegations and language-help box
Exercises 50.1–50.5 and Unit 50 answer key, including journalistic collocations and semantic contrasts

items.example: Print journalism has adapted its reporting schedules to a digital news cycle.
items.note: Reporting for newspapers and magazines; distinct from broadcast or online journalism.

items.example: She studied broadcast journalism before joining a national radio station.
items.note: News reporting for radio or television, often involving live audio or video.

items.example: Online journalism can update an article as new evidence emerges.
items.note: News published through websites or digital platforms; not necessarily citizen journalism.

items.pt: jornalismo cidadão; cobertura feita por pessoas comuns
items.example: Citizen journalism helped document events that professional reporters could not attend.
items.note: Reporting or sharing news by members of the public rather than necessarily by employed journalists.

items.pt: grupo de pressão; organização de defesa de uma causa
items.example: A pressure group urged ministers to publish the environmental assessment.
items.note: Organisation seeking to influence decisions or public opinion around a particular issue.

items.example: Local residents were invited to air their views at a public meeting.
items.note: Air means state or express openly, often to an audience or the press.

items.example: The mayor answered questions about the funding decision at a press conference.
items.note: An event where journalists receive information and can ask questions.

items.example: The organisation issued a statement correcting the earlier report.
items.note: Issue is a formal reporting verb meaning release or publish a statement.

items.example: The museum circulated a press release announcing its renovation.
items.note: Written information officially supplied to news organisations; unlike a conference, it need not involve questions.

items.example: The campaign sought publicity to attract potential volunteers.
items.note: Publicity is public attention; seek publicity is not necessarily the same as buy advertising.

items.pt: frase curta e marcante usada pela imprensa
items.example: The candidate prepared a memorable soundbite for the television interview.
items.note: A brief quotable phrase or recorded extract, often repeated by news programmes.

items.example: Investigative reporters hunt for stories by examining public records.
items.note: Informal figurative use of hunt for: actively look for potential reports.

items.pt: recorrer a fontes úteis; explorar fontes de informação
items.example: The reporter tapped useful sources in several research institutions.
items.note: Tap means make use of an existing source of information, not secretly intercept communications.

items.example: The publication confirmed the announcement with an international news agency.
items.note: Organisation supplying news reports to outlets, often via subscription or syndication.

items.example: The team monitored the news for updates on the court ruling.
items.note: Monitor means regularly observe or check for developments.

items.pt: tempo de exposição no rádio ou na televisão
items.example: The investigation received substantial airtime on the evening bulletin.
items.note: Time devoted to a topic or speaker on radio or television; not printed page space.

items.pt: espaço ocupado por uma matéria no jornal impresso
items.example: The local election received fewer column inches than the football final.
items.note: Traditional measure of newspaper space, not television airtime.

items.example: The floods received extensive news coverage across the country.
items.note: Media attention to a story, whether in print, online or broadcasting.

items.example: Paparazzi gathered outside the venue hoping to photograph the actor.
items.note: Usually plural; informal, often disapproving word for photographers pursuing public figures.

items.example: He dismissed the sensationalist paper as a rag.
items.note: Informal and insulting noun for a newspaper thought to have little credibility.

items.example: The minister accused the gutter press of exploiting private family problems.
items.note: Disapproving collective phrase for sensationalist publications focused on scandal.

items.example: Reporters must produce copy that editors can check before publication.
items.note: Copy is written material prepared for print or publication, not a photocopy.

items.pt: cumprir o prazo de fechamento ou entrega
items.example: The reporter worked overnight to meet the deadline for the morning edition.
items.note: Meet a deadline means finish by the required time; journalists also refer to tight deadlines.

items.example: The newsroom faced a tight deadline after the late announcement.
items.note: A very short or demanding time limit for completing work.

items.pt: entrar em impressão; fechar a edição para a gráfica
items.example: The editor corrected the headline just before the issue went to press.
items.note: Fixed expression for a publication reaching the production stage of printing.

items.pt: edições anteriores de jornal ou revista
items.example: The library keeps back copies of the newspaper for historical research.
items.note: Old issues of a publication; do not confuse with new copies or backup files.

items.example: The newspaper’s online archive contains articles dating back decades.
items.note: A searchable collection of older content; archive is not always the same as a live news feed.

items.pt: matéria exclusiva; notícia divulgada por um único veículo
items.example: The editor announced an exclusive based on documents obtained by the team.
items.note: As a journalism noun, a story reported by one outlet first or alone.

items.pt: furo de reportagem; notícia exclusiva obtida antes de outros veículos
items.example: The reporter won an award for a major political scoop.
items.note: Informal noun for important exclusive information or a story obtained ahead of competitors.

items.example: The broadcaster decided to run the story after checking the evidence.
items.note: Run is a reporting verb: a newspaper, channel or website runs a story.

items.pt: virar manchete; ganhar destaque no noticiário
items.example: The inquiry hit the headlines when new documents were released.
items.note: Idiomatic expression meaning become major news; the story is already public at that point.

items.pt: uma notícia vem a público; o caso é revelado
items.example: When the story breaks, the team will publish its full investigation.
items.note: Break describes the first public emergence of news; not a physical break.

items.pt: difamação por meio de publicação; difamação escrita
items.section: B · Editorial framing and reputational harm
items.example: The newspaper faced a libel claim over an unsupported accusation.
items.note: Traditional legal term for reputational harm by a published false statement; rules vary by jurisdiction.

items.pt: difamação; ataque à reputação de alguém
items.section: B · Editorial framing and reputational harm
items.example: The actor filed a complaint alleging defamation of character.
items.note: Broader reputational-harm concept than libel in the textbook: may encompass written and spoken forms.

items.pt: difamação oral; declaração falada que prejudica a reputação
items.section: B · Editorial framing and reputational harm
items.example: The public accusation led to a dispute over alleged slander.
items.note: Traditionally spoken defamation, contrasted with published or written libel; a related distinction in the answer key.

items.section: B · Editorial framing and reputational harm
items.example: Readers of different political persuasions reacted differently to the editorial.
items.note: Persuasion here means a set of beliefs or affiliations, not the act of convincing someone.

items.word: put a gloss on a story
items.pt: dar uma interpretação interessada a uma notícia
items.section: B · Editorial framing and reputational harm
items.example: The spokesperson put a favourable gloss on the disappointing figures.
items.note: Present events from a particular, often self-serving perspective; gloss overlaps with spin.

items.word: put your own spin on events
items.pt: dar sua própria versão ou enquadramento aos acontecimentos
items.section: B · Editorial framing and reputational harm
items.example: Commentators put their own spin on the court’s decision.
items.note: Spin suggests selective framing or interpretation, sometimes with a manipulative implication.

items.pt: investigação de escândalos; exploração de histórias comprometedoras
items.section: B · Editorial framing and reputational harm
items.example: Critics accused the tabloid of muck-raking instead of examining public policy.
items.note: Disapproving in this context; also may describe the exposure of genuine wrongdoing.

items.pt: heroico; apresentado como ato de grande coragem
items.section: B · Editorial framing and reputational harm
items.example: The newspaper described the rescue as a heroic effort by volunteers.
items.note: Dramatic positive adjective; journalistic usage can exaggerate ordinary actions.

items.section: B · Editorial framing and reputational harm
items.example: The headline called the small fundraising success a triumph.
items.note: Strong noun for a major success; in headlines it may be exaggerated for effect.

items.section: B · Editorial framing and reputational harm
items.example: Minor power interruptions were once a frequent occurrence in the area.
items.note: A relatively neutral noun for something that happens, unlike triumph or disaster.

items.pt: a mídia; os meios de comunicação
items.example: The media have questioned the accuracy of the original report.
items.note: Often takes a plural verb in formal British usage; collective singular forms also occur, especially with social media.

items.pt: atenção da mídia; repercussão na imprensa
items.example: The campaign attracted considerable media attention following the announcement.
items.note: Media is an attributive modifier here, like in media reports or media coverage.

items.example: The start-up failed to meet expectations created by months of media hype.
items.note: Hype suggests excessive publicity or inflated claims, often critically.

items.word: air your views to the press
items.example: The councillor was keen to air her views to the press after the vote.
items.note: Source-backed extended collocation; air opinions to the press, rather than air on a press.

items.pt: boletim de notícias; edição curta de noticiário
items.example: The radio station interrupted the music for an urgent news bulletin.
items.note: A short broadcast summarising current news; mentioned in the source explanation of soundbites.
